articles.title_orig: California probing whether China improperly got Nvidia technology
articles.title_zh: California probing whether China improperly got Nvidia technology
articles.content_orig:
California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.
The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.
Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.
Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating  Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.
Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs – and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO live: Anthropic stock closes up 17% from initial price for $1.27T valuation in first day of trading
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO live: Anthropic stock closes up 17% from initial price for $1.27T valuation in first day of trading
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic's stock soared in early trading on Nasdaq Thursday before partly shedding those gains in the afternoon, as the artificial intelligence developer completed the largest initial public offering in history.
Trading under the ticker "ANT," Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, up 34% from the $83 offer price, and rose as high as $114.99, valuing the company at more than $2 trillion at the peak. The stock pared those gains over the course of the day, closing at $97.17, a rise of 17%.
"Both the jump from the offer price and the high volatility are not surprising, given the enormous potential of the company and the wildly different opinions about how profitable the company will become," Jay Ritter, an IPO expert and professor at the University of Florida's Warrington College of Business, said in an email.
Anthropic shares rose on a day when the rest of the stock market took a dive. Late in Thursday's session, the Nasdaq dropped 550 points, or 2.3%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled more than 1,100 points, or 2.2%, and the S&P 500 sank 2%.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei celebrated Anthropic's market debut at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City on Thursday.
"The goal is to make the whole industry better, regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time," Dario Amodei said Thursday in an event to mark the IPO.
"The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history, and we have a rare opportunity to shape it for the better," he added.
San Francisco-based Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in its IPO, catapulting past SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it went public in June. The IPO values the company behind the Claude chatbot at roughly $1.5 trillion, more than companies such as Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway, JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Walmart.
Anthropic's IPO represents an "A-plus success," Dan Ives, a tech analyst and partner of Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News. "I think it's a vote of confidence for the market relative to the tech trade," he added.
The public offering delivered a huge payday to the seven Anthropic co-founders, boosting their worth on paper to around $20 billion each. It will also turn many Anthropic employees into millionaires.
Anthropic said Wednesday that it would offer 980 million shares of Class A common stock priced at $83 per share, allowing it to raise a record-breaking amount. Anthropic originally priced its shares in a range of $70 to $78, but raised its per-share IPO price amid strong investor demand.
The IPO price of $83 a share is what Anthropic insiders and other early investors pay to receive an allocation of stock. According to investment bank Renaissance Capital, 7.4% of Anthropic shares are available for public trading (or up to 9.8% if Class A shares held by non-founder employees are included).
Even if Americans don't buy shares, Anthropic's IPO could still affect their 401(k) , given how exposed the stock market is to AI stocks.
Anthropic has previously said it will raise an additional $26 billion from a slate of other companies, including chipmaker AMD, chip infrastructure provider Broadcom, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, bringing its fundraising total to around $107 billion.
Matthew Kennedy, a senior market strategist at Renaissance Capital, thinks Anthropic shares could reach $100 by the end of their first day of trading.
However, like many companies that go public in a blockbuster, and perhaps overhyped, share offering, Anthropic's stock could well waver in the months to come. In a Truist study of 32 of the biggest ever IPOs, more than half saw their shares slide by at least 50% at some point during their first year of trading.
Anthropic announced its plans to go public in October, inviting investors to be part of what it called one of the "seminal moments in human history." The company is the first frontier AI lab to go public.
Anthropic's IPO comes at a critical time for the AI industry, as investors are asking harder questions about the sector's growing losses, capital investments and returns, Sam Grelck, an equity strategy analyst at Truist Advisory Services, a unit of Truist Financial, told CBS News.
"I wouldn't view Anthropic's IPO as a verdict on AI, but the reception can give us another indication of investors' appetite for the AI theme after what's been a challenging few weeks," he said.
AI-related stocks have swung sharply in recent weeks as concerns mount about the mountainous debt companies are taking on to finance the data center buildout and a potential Democratic-led crackdown on the AI boom following the midterms . Jensen Huang's shock exit from Nvidia last week has also rattled investors.
At a time when investors are skittish, the robust demand for Anthropic shares suggests there is still faith that lofty investments in AI will pay off.
"Anthropic's IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Ives said in a research note.
The IPO provides Anthropic with cash to finance its AI development plans . The company, which is yet to turn a profit, has said it wants to use its technology to "improve how humans live" by providing tailored financial and legal advice and speeding up scientific discovery.
"I believe sufficient and powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of medical and scientific progress into a decade," Amodei said at Nasdaq in New York on Thursday.
While the IPO will boost its coffers, Anthropic could quickly burn through cash as it works to keep its AI models on the cutting edge and stay ahead of rivals like OpenAI.
As of Sept. 30, the company had $6.2 billion in debt, according to its regulatory filing. At the same time, it has committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on chips and AI infrastructure through 2045.

articles.title_orig: California AG issues subpoena to Nvidia in probe of China chips
articles.title_zh: California AG issues subpoena to Nvidia in probe of China chips
articles.content_orig:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta has issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia as part of a probe of whether the company's advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China i n contravention of U.S. export restrictions, his office said Thursday.
The probe comes a week after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy. Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that is being investigation for potentially diverting restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," Bonta said in a statement.
"My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law," Bonta said.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," the attorney general said.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bonta's subpoena.
Nvidia shares are down 22% in the nine trading days since Huang admitted to an extramarital affair. The stock is on pace for its seventh straight weekly loss, shedding 38% of its value over that stretch.

articles.title_orig: Trump says he and China's Xi want moderate AI rules
articles.title_zh: Trump says he and China's Xi want moderate AI rules
articles.content_orig:
By DAVID WILCOCK, DEPUTY POLITICAL EDITOR and JASON GROVES, POLITICAL EDITOR
Published: 06:09 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 08:59 EST, 19 November 2026
Andy Burnham will join European leaders in a show of solidarity with Ukraine today, hours after Donald Trump took part in an astonishing summit with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping .
The Prime Minister is chairing a meeting of 'Coalition of the Willing' countries in Berlin after announcing Britain will supply a further 1,000 long-range strike drones to Kyiv and jointly fund two £100 million attack boats with Norway.
But the meeting will have to deal with the fallout from the meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China in Shenzhen.
Ministers were already nervous that the US President could agree a stitch-up that weakens Ukraine as the war with Russia enters another winter.
He greeted Putin by describing him as a 'friend' with whom he was 'really making history', adding: 'No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.'
Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said the three countries have 'numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine'.
The Prime Minister, pictured with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, will co-chair a meeting of 'Coalition of the Willing' countries in Berlin
But the meeting will have to deal with the fallout from the meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China in Shenzhen
Speaking in the Commons yesterday, Mr Burnham declined to comment on the Shenzhen summit directly, but said: 'When that meeting is taking place in China I will be in Berlin for a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing.
'The thing that we need to do is continue to stand squarely by Ukraine, and that is what this Government will do.'
He said that Britain was united in its support for Ukraine, adding: 'On this issue, let that clear message go out as that meeting takes place in China: this country is squarely with Ukraine.
'We know who the aggressor is in this situation, and we will not in any way deflect from continuing that support.'
The PM last night unveiled a £260million package of direct support for Ukraine.
The package includes 1,000 long-range drones capable of delivering heavy warheads to strike military targets at distances of more than 600 miles.
Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said the three countries have 'numerous shared interests'
The UK will also build and deliver maritime, logistical and surveillance drones to assist Ukraine in resupplying frontline forces with vital supplies like blood and fridges to hold medicines.
It follows agreement in recent days for Britain to bolster Ukraine's air defences and impose tighter sanctions on Russian oil producers.
The move comes as Putin targets civilian infrastructure in a bid to break Ukrainian morale during the cruel winter months when temperatures regularly drop to minus 20 degrees.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has faced more than 2,000 Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure, leaving civilians without heat or power.
In parts of the country, including the capital Kyiv, energy and water blackouts are now a daily occurrence, sometimes lasting up to 22 hours at a time as engineers battle to restore supplies.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: 'Putin uses winter as a weapon in Ukraine. We are converting our steadfast commitment for Ukraine into capability that will help defend against Russia's barbaric attacks on civilians.
'Ukraine's frontline is the frontline for freedom and democracy, and we will stand with them for as long as it takes.'

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi, Putin sit down for a rare meeting in China
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi, Putin sit down for a rare meeting in China
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries, but there appeared to be little concrete to show for the meeting in terms of resolving any of the crises facing the world.
The leaders offered a joint statement after their roughly hour-and-a-half-long meeting. Mr. Trump immediately left for his return flight to the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. On the flight home, the president said on social media he will hold a press conference at noon on Friday to discuss the trip.
The presidents discussed Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine , which Mr. Trump has wanted to bring to a negotiated end. But the only significant statement on the conflict came after the meeting from Putin, who ruled out any direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing a major strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces on a key bridge in Russian-held Crimea.
Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it called a joint statement from all three leaders characterizing the talks. The White House later provided the same statement.
The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."
They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the " International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."
Finally, the leaders "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."
The White House indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.
The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.
Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine, who sits on the Committee on Foreign Relations, said the image of Mr. Trump standing with Xi and Putin was concerning.
"Some of the pictures troubled me, seeing the president stand with Putin and Xi, rather than seeing the president stand with the leaders of the global democracies," Kaine said. "When I saw them, it turned my stomach a bit, and particularly President Trump's declaration that Vladimir Putin was a friend. Vladimir Putin is not a friend, and so you know he was either being insincere or he is deeply deluded if he thinks Vladimir Putin is a friend."
In a phone call with NBC reporter Gabe Gutierrez, Mr. Trump called the meeting a 12 on a scale of zero to 10.
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
After the trilateral talks Thursday, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.
"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."
Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia  in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."
Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."
Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons , with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.
Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program , ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year .
China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi , however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."
The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.
A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence .
The summit took place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang , whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed , is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.
Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.
Mr. Trump brought up AI during a speech at the APEC forum earlier in the day, vowing to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial int

articles.title_orig: Kushner says he believes Russia is ‘comfortable’ with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Kushner says he believes Russia is ‘comfortable’ with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
European leaders of the so-called “Coalition of the Willing” gathered in the German capital for talks intended to signal a united front in support of Ukraine.
The Berlin meeting happened hours after an unprecedented three-way summit in Shenzhen, China, between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.
Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the Shenzhen meeting a “photo op”, warning that any deal made without Europe at the table would fail.
Merz said that “if it comes to peace negotiations, then we will be involved”, adding that such talks “can only be successful with Ukraine and Europe”.
Merz said he hoped to work as a “team with Kyiv and Washington” when they hold talks with Russia on ending the Ukraine war, although no announcement of when that would be has been made.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Europe is “ready to enter negotiations”, insisting that “a peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia must come first”.
“Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position,” Burnham added.
European countries have been angered after the European Union was largely sidelined in the United States’ stop-start negotiations with Russia and Ukraine.
However, Donald Trump’s son-in-law and peace envoy Jared Kushner said, “Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side.”
Kushner said, “We do believe that Russia having Europe at the table will be essential for ending the war.”
Russia is “comfortable”, Kushner added, with the idea of security guarantees for postwar Ukraine modelled on NATO’s Article 5, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
“I think we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” he said, adding that Trump was “open” to the idea but that “obviously it has to be in America’s interest” and part of “a broader security package”.
It was not clear what form any guarantees would take, or whether Russia and Ukraine would accept them. Russia has not commented on Kushner’s claim.
Kushner said Trump called into the Berlin talks after his meeting with Putin, and that the last round of talks, in Abu Dhabi last week, produced no major breakthrough.
The British prime minister welcomed the US presence at talks in Berlin, saying it added momentum to end the war.
“This clearly has got to be a moment ⁠to move towards ⁠peace because of the US involvement that we’ve ⁠seen today and ⁠the progress clearly ⁠that is being made,” Burnham said.
Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron called on Ukraine’s allies to ramp up efforts to end the war.
“Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now,” he insisted, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
“Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to NATO,” Macron said. NATO membership for Ukraine is among the issues holding back a peace deal for Ukraine.
In a post on X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, “We do not want Russia to drag all of this out into the winter. Pressure is needed. Europe is ready with new sanctions and new steps to support Ukraine and the Ukrainian people. It is important that the United States of America exert its influence on Russia.”
Speaking to reporters in Shenzhen, Putin vowed to retaliate for what he called serious damage to the Kerch Bridge, which links occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland, in three Ukrainian aerial attacks this week.
“We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Putin said.
He said the road section was “seriously damaged” but would be rebuilt, and that the bridge was a civilian asset that he had ordered closed to military hardware and ammunition.
Train traffic resumed on Thursday afternoon, RIA Novosti reported. Ukraine’s Defence Ministry said Russia would now have to move fuel and ammunition over land, “where our drones are waiting for the cargo”.
Putin said the Kremlin was not against European participation in peace talks and even proposed they be held in the Russian capital.
He said Moscow had proposed, through diplomatic channels, that European officials come to Moscow “to determine their position”, without setting a date.
Overnight, Russia’s Defence Ministry said it intercepted 53 Ukrainian drones. A Ukrainian attack on Russia’s Saratov region killed three people, local governor Roman Busargin said, and Ukraine said Russian anti-ship missiles and 98 drones hit 18 locations, killing two people and wounding at least 23.
Minor damage was reported at the Dutch and Austrian embassies in Kyiv.
The Netherlands summoned Russia’s ambassador in The Hague after the incident in which a projectile landed behind the building on Thursday afternoon. No one was hurt.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen told the broadcaster RTL the incident was “unacceptable”.
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said Austria’s embassy in Kyiv was also hit, with no staff harmed, and Sweden said it would summon Russia’s ambassador over an explosion near its embassy, Reuters reported.
Russia’s embassy in the Netherlands had said earlier on Thursday that it was becoming “increasingly difficult to regard the Netherlands as a mere bystander” in the war. That followed a statement by the Dutch defence company Destinus that its missiles were the only foreign-made weapons used in Ukraine’s attack on the Kerch Bridge on Tuesday.
It was unclear whether the embassy incident was related.

articles.title_orig: Leaders of China, Russia, US praise trilateral summit as 'success'
articles.title_zh: Leaders of China, Russia, US praise trilateral summit as 'success'
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months
articles.title_zh: US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months
articles.content_orig:
The administration of United States President Donald Trump approved exports of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee has said.
The Department of Commerce’s approvals covered exports of 879,000 chips, including 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD, the committee said on Thursday.
Companies had sought permission to ship 3.4 million of them to China during the period, committee documents show.
The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the Trump administration faces heightened scrutiny following revelations about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy , which fuelled renewed calls for a tougher stance against Chinese technology threats.
All four of the Chinese companies highlighted in the committee report are on the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies.
The committee chair, Brian Mast, has “exercised his authorities under the Export Control Reform Act to publicly reveal export control license application information regarding NVIDIA and AMD’s AI chip licenses for the People’s Republic of China”, the committee said in a statement. It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of the chips, which included Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent MI325X.
News surrounding Huang has turned a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialling up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats.
“The fact that over 30 percent of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses,” said Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle.
Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were “subject to strict conditions and limited volumes”. It added that “despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China”.
AMD did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Former US President Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China’s military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence.
But Trump in December gave the green light for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum.
Nvidia’s stock ended the day down 3.3 percent, while AMD slumped 7.7 percent and the broader Nasdaq and S&P 500 were down 2.2 percent and 1.8 percent, respectively.

articles.title_zh: Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Customer Data Leaked by Hackers
articles.content_orig:
Payment services were unaffected, the companies said.
JPMorganChase said Thursday morning that "third parties who provide services" to the banking giant "were the target of a cyberattack."
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," the statement continued.
"There is no disruption to our services," according to the statement.
JPMorganChase, the largest U.S. bank, did not disclose when the cyberattack occurred or name the third-party companies that were targeted.
"Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring," the company said in its statement.
JPMorganChase said on Monday that it experienced technical issues that triggered online delays across several major U.S. banks and blamed the outage on a "software bug." The company said Thursday that it found "no connection to service disruptions some customers experienced earlier this week" regarding the third-party provider data breach.
Mastercard also reported on Thursday that one of its third-party providers was hacked, while Visa said earlier this week that it was aware that one of its third-party providers experienced a data breach.
"They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific," Visa said in its statement. "Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected."
"We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of [a] limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," Mastercard said in its statement Thursday.
"There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," Mastercard further said. "At this time, the exposure has been contained, and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed."
There have been several recent tech outages across the nation that affected air travel, email and hotel reservations, and even slowed classified internal communications at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration officials continued this week to insist that there is no evidence that those outages were the result of cyberattacks.

articles.title_orig: Appeals court grants Trump request to halt order restoring Venezuelan TPS
articles.title_zh: Appeals court grants Trump request to halt order restoring Venezuelan TPS
articles.content_orig:
A United States appeals court has allowed the administration of President Donald Trump to move forward for now with the removal of deportation protections for Venezuelans .
The ruling on Wednesday cancels out a previous order by a lower-court judge that required the government to restore the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) of Venezuelans, which shields recipients against deportation.
The effort to end the TPS protections has proceeded despite humanitarian concerns .
Since taking office for a second term, Trump has sought to carry out what he calls the largest deportation effort in US history. Part of that agenda has been to roll back programmes like TPS.
But in September 2025, US District Judge Edward Chen blocked the expiration of TPS protections for Venezuelans, arguing that deporting those individuals would put them in harm’s way.
He also ruled that the Trump administration had overstepped its authority by seeking to shorten TPS extensions granted under the preceding president, Joe Biden. Such decisions, Chen added, needed to be taken with “careful study and analysis”.
Some 600,000 Venezuelans in the US were protected under TPS programmes.
The Supreme Court paused Chen’s ruling in October 2025. But that pause expired this month, and Chen’s order was set to take effect on Friday.
On Wednesday, the Trump administration filed an emergency request to the Supreme Court to extend the pause before Thursday’s appeals court ruling.
The appeals court’s decision does not nix the ongoing legal challenges to Trump’s efforts to revoke TPS extensions. But it allows the administration to suspend deportation protections while the challenges make their way through court.
The Trump administration has sought to strip large numbers of immigrants of their legal protections in a bid to render them deportable. Other programmes, like humanitarian parole, have also come under the administration’s scrutiny.
TPS allows foreign nationals already in the US to remain while conditions in their home countries are too dangerous or unstable to return to.
Humanitarian parole, meanwhile, allows people outside the US to come in on a temporary basis, often to escape similarly perilous conditions.
The Trump administration has argued that TPS designations are meant to be temporary — and that previous presidencies extended such protections without cause.
It has also maintained that conditions have improved in places like Venezuela, where a US military action on January 3 resulted in the abduction of President Nicolas Maduro.
Human rights advocates, however, have noted that Maduro’s government remains largely intact. That leadership has been accused of abuses ranging from arbitrary imprisonment to the torture of political dissidents.
The US Department of State currently warns against travel to Venezuela, citing issues such as crime, kidnapping and poor health infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: Trump China trip: Iran and Ukraine not in 'peace declaration' and more takeaways - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Trump China trip: Iran and Ukraine not in 'peace declaration' and more takeaways - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
“It’s not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up,” Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The “peace declaration” released after the meeting made no mention of Russia’s war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."

Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."
Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."
The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."
Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.
AMD continued to slide after-hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SHENZHEN, China — Donald Trump met Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a villa in southern China, an unprecedented gathering of a U.S. president with Washington’s chief geopolitical rivals bent on undermining American power.
The meeting, conceived not by policymakers but by Trump and Putin themselves, had a fractured agenda, with each leader coming to the table with divergent interests and different stakes .
But the image of Trump standing alongside Putin and Xi — then sitting alone with the two of them, at a great round table in a cacophonous hall — was itself the culmination of a decade of his foreign policy thinking , a great-man theory of diplomacy that has broken with American tradition, elevating authoritarian leaders over democratic allies.
The U.S. president appeared subdued, thanking Xi and Putin before turning to the press.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” he said, arguing he had a “special responsibility” to maintain dialogue with adversarial world powers. “We are really making history.”
Unlike at Yalta, in 1945, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Josef Stalin famously gathered to shape the postwar order, the American leader was not at the center of these photographs. That place of honor belonged to Xi, the host, who presided over the gathering at a remote retreat outside the city.
It was a portrait of a nation asserting its place among the world’s superpowers — the very image Beijing had sought in agreeing to host the extraordinary gathering.
“History tells us that when great powers are at peace, the world is secure,” Xi said. “When great powers clash, the world is in chaos.”
The competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that harken back to the famous Yalta conference of 1945.
It was not immediately clear when the meeting concluded, after roughly an hour and a half, whether the three leaders had reached any substantive understandings. They were expected to discuss arms control and the wars in Iran and Ukraine, among other matters.
An initial readout of the meeting first released by the Russian side listed four points of agreement, broadly committing to work to uphold international security, minimize nuclear risks, increase petroleum output and, most specifically,  overhaul the United Nations and the International Criminal Court, which it said “must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
The court has a warrant outstanding for Putin’s arrest.
Putin framed the trilateral meeting as one of equals, elevating a Russian Federation that has been economically and militarily devastated, and ostracized from the international community, over its war against Ukraine. Russian state media highlighted Xi’s decision to place Putin to his right throughout the summit as a gesture of honor.
“I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, our peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world,” Putin said, “if they cooperate constructively as partners on the basis of mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests.”
The Russian leader appeared almost giddy throughout the day’s meetings, and upon departing Shenzhen for the airport, escorted personally by Xi to his car, was heard saying, “I don’t think anyone ever expected everything to go so well.”
“The trilateral summit was a giant gift to Putin. It put him on a stage where he does not belong,” Michael McFaul, a former U.S. ambassador to Russia now at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, told The Times. “The photo of that meeting will be seen throughout the world, making it look like Putin is a respected leader of a great power. What did Americans get in return? Nothing, absolutely nothing.”
The unusual summit comes just weeks after Trump suffered a generational rebuke in the midterm elections and as he remains bogged down in a war with Iran, which threatened to erupt in a new round of hostilities in the coming days.
Publicly, Trump framed the gathering as an effort to curb nuclear proliferation. Yet instead of advancing a trilateral nonproliferation agreement among the world’s three largest nuclear powers, Putin offered a message of defiance, sending nuclear-capable bombers to nearby Vietnam a day before the summit in a rare deployment. China, meanwhile, rebuffed calls to slow down its breakneck nuclear buildup currently dwarfed by America’s arsenal.
The Trump administration let the last remaining U.S. arms control agreement with Russia expire earlier this year.
“Despite the talk of denuclearization by the Trump administration, no staff members prepped the president to meaningfully discuss this topic with Putin or Xi, who are unwilling partners for restraints and guardrails,” said Jennifer Hong, senior director of the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security.
Instead, Trump’s focus seems to have turned to ensuring nonproliferation not among world powers, but in the Middle East — the main justification he has given for launching war against Tehran earlier this year.
“We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said at the top of the meeting.
Putin had hoped the summit would secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine — a prospect that Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, took seriously as the meeting was about to begin.
“Big countries always think that they can make decisions about the future of all the world,” Zelensky told NBC News. “It’s a huge mistake.”
Sitting alongside Xi, Trump said the two of them were looking to “help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine” and “would like to see it ended.”
Few independent analysts believe Putin is interested in ending the war in its current state. But at the trilateral engagement, Trump suggested Zelensky was responsible for Moscow’s continued attempts at conquest. “Things are happening,” Trump said. “I think that he, and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war.”
The meetings were Trump’s first with Putin since the two held a summit last year in Alaska, a gathering that failed to produce a breakthrough in Trump’s attempts to bring an end to the deadliest conflict in Europe since World War II.
Trump met individually with both Putin and Xi ahead of the trilateral gathering, despite White House officials insisting before the trip that a direct meeting with Putin was not on the agenda.
“Who is he? He’s my friend,” Trump said, walking toward Putin with an outstretched hand.
“We have had a great relationship for many years. We’ve known each other for a long time,” Trump added. “And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start.”
A Russian diplomat attending the conference with Putin told reporters that Trump and Putin together are “committed to a peaceful resolution to the Ukrainian conflict, though the Europeans are clearly trying to stand in the way.”
European officials have been wary of the Shenzhen summit, warning against the future of Ukraine being negotiated without Ukrainians present. A Chinese official told The Times they would have been welcome to attend, but no invitation was formally extended.
Xi greeted Trump at the steps of Air Force One upon his arrival in Shenzhen on Wednesday evening, reciprocating the rare honor Trump extended to the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington in September.
While Trump’s meetings with Xi were the primary purpose of his visit, the Chinese leader is also hosting a major international conference, gathering leaders from around the world for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, known as APEC.

articles.content_orig:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen , south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.
In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."
But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".
Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.
Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.
Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."
The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.
He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.
"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.
Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.
The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.
There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.
But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.
It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.
As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.
And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.
He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.
Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.
"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.
Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

articles.title_orig: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
articles.title_zh: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
articles.content_orig:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

articles.title_orig: AMD Stock Drops After Short Report Says It Isn’t an Nvidia Replacement
articles.title_zh: AMD Stock Drops After Short Report Says It Isn’t an Nvidia Replacement
articles.content_orig:
Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."
Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."
The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."
Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.
AMD continued to slide after-hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

articles.title_orig: Commerce approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, Rep. Mast says
articles.title_zh: Commerce approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, Rep. Mast says
articles.content_orig:
The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, there had been 3.4 million requested sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices .
"Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents.
The Commerce Department, AMD and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
"The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks continued.
The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest." The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including Bytedance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu .
The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China.
In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.
Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS —  Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions.
"Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting.
Maginfra and New Matrix did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2.
Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify.
Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third controls.
The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.
This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.
— Megan Cassella and Daren Fonda contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Google turns to Blue Origin for a rocket, but its long-term problem remains
articles.title_zh: Google turns to Blue Origin for a rocket, but its long-term problem remains
articles.content_orig:
Blue Origin announced Thursday that its New Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that company’s Project Suncatcher program.
Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers about a year ago and characterized the project as one of its research “moonshots.” The mission on New Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy.
“Project Suncatcher is a long-term moonshot to scale AI infrastructure in space by tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit,” said Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher at Google, in the news release. “This dedicated launch with Blue Origin represents a crucial milestone on our roadmap as we expand the boundaries of what’s possible for the future of compute.”
The announcement comes as US commercial heavy lift rockets, including New Glenn, are filling up their capacity through the year 2030. The Google mission will fly on the 7×2 variant of the New Glenn rocket, the smaller version of the vehicle that has launched three times to date.
The purpose of the 2029 launch will likely be to test the ability to network solar-powered satellites equipped with AI chips and demonstrate machine-learning compute in space. In that sense, it will be a technology demonstration. Google did not say who it was contracting with to build the satellites, which may weigh something on the order of several tons.
Perhaps the bigger question for Google is not whether it can make this technology work—but whether it is tenable for a company to have ambitions for a large constellation of orbital data centers in the 2030s without its own launch vehicle.
There remain a lot of questions about the economic viability of orbital data centers, but almost everyone agrees on one universal truth: Without ultra low-cost, heavy lift capability, there is no way that data centers in space can be economically competitive with terrestrial data centers.
Upon announcing Project Suncatcher a year ago, Google said it was planning for the mid-2030s, when launch costs are projected to drop to as little as $200 per kg. The only rocket likely capable of reaching those costs during the next decade is SpaceX’s Starship vehicle, but in recent months it has become clear that SpaceX will prioritize its own payloads (including Starmind data centers) on Starship. For Google to reach its target price of $200 per kg, it would likely require a fully optimized Starship V4 (the company is currently flying a V3 Starship) that reaches a lift capacity of approximately 200 metric tons to orbit.
SpaceX has powerful incentives to prioritize its own orbital computing infrastructure, potentially leaving Google dependent on whatever Starship capacity and pricing SpaceX is willing to offer outside customers. So how does Google plan to reach orbit in the 2030s?
Perhaps this explains the new partnership with Blue Origin, which presently covers a single launch but could grow to more. By the 2030s Blue Origin should be flying the larger 9×4 variant of its New Glenn rocket, but this vehicle could face a cost disadvantage against a fully reusable, high-cadence Starship. And Blue Origin is planning its own orbital data center constellation, Project Sunrise . So again, Google could be stuck subsidizing a competitor while paying higher launch costs.
Perhaps another company, such as Rocket Lab, Relativity Space, or Stoke Space, will have a larger rocket by then.
But developing a super-heavy-lift rocket requires enormous capital. SpaceX has spent more than $15 billion developing Starship, according to its 2026 securities filings, and Blue Origin has likewise invested billions in developing New Glenn. In terms of time, both companies have put more than a decade of work into their large vehicles. For now, all of these other US launch companies are working through the growing pains of developing medium-lift vehicles.
At this point, Google has some not-great options. It can hope that one of the newer US launch companies steps up for commercial satellite operators and decides not to pursue its own constellation. It could buy one of those newer launch companies. Or Google could hire some rocket scientists to start developing powerful rocket engines and begin chasing SpaceX and Blue Origin in launch—both of which have a 25-year head start.
