articles.title_orig: Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ summit with Putin and Xi, though peace deals remain elusive
articles.title_zh: Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ summit with Putin and Xi, though peace deals remain elusive
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries, but there appeared to be little concrete to show for the meeting in terms of resolving any of the crises facing the world.
The leaders offered a joint statement after their roughly hour-and-a-half-long meeting. Mr. Trump immediately left for his return flight to the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. On the flight home, the president said on social media he will hold a press conference at noon on Friday to discuss the trip.
The presidents discussed Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine , which Mr. Trump has wanted to bring to a negotiated end. But the only significant statement on the conflict came after the meeting from Putin, who ruled out any direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing a major strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces on a key bridge in Russian-held Crimea.
Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it called a joint statement from all three leaders characterizing the talks. The White House later provided the same statement.
The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."
They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the " International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."
Finally, the leaders "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."
The White House indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.
The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.
Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine, who sits on the Committee on Foreign Relations, said the image of Mr. Trump standing with Xi and Putin was concerning.
"Some of the pictures troubled me, seeing the president stand with Putin and Xi, rather than seeing the president stand with the leaders of the global democracies," Kaine said. "When I saw them, it turned my stomach a bit, and particularly President Trump's declaration that Vladimir Putin was a friend. Vladimir Putin is not a friend, and so you know he was either being insincere or he is deeply deluded if he thinks Vladimir Putin is a friend."
In a phone call with NBC reporter Gabe Gutierrez, Mr. Trump called the meeting a 12 on a scale of zero to 10.
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
After the trilateral talks Thursday, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.
"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."
Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia  in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."
Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."
Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons , with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.
Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program , ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year .
China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi , however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."
The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.
A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence .
The summit took place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang , whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed , is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.
Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.

articles.title_orig: There’s Comfort In Conquering The Past
articles.title_zh: There’s Comfort In Conquering The Past
articles.content_orig:
2:34 PM EST on November 19, 2026
The first time I played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was during a hurricane. It was late 1999, I was 10 years old, Hurricane Irene was bearing down on Miami, and my friend Ryan had come over to spend the night. He had brought his copy of Ocarina of Time , the game a year old at that point, and his plan was that we should play it all the way to the end. This was a bold goal for two idiot preteen boys, and though we plowed through the entire Child Link part of the game and the start of Adult Link's quest to release the temple sages, the Water Temple claimed us as its own. We didn't have a Prima strategy guide or the internet to help us out, so after hours (and I do mean hours) of raising and lowering water levels, we gave up. I didn't end up beating my own copy of Ocarina of Time , which my dad bought for me as soon as the hurricane passed, until the next summer in Venezuela, but even then, even as an idiot preteen boy, I knew I had played something special.
Twenty-seven years later, I am playing something special again. Well, I am playing the same thing again, but newer, fresher, and more beautiful. I am playing the remake of Ocarina of Time , and I have loved every second of it so far. As a remake, this is a work of art. The graphics are gorgeous, if a bit shiny. The story is as good as it ever was, only now with a lot more voice acting that gives characters personality. The gameplay is much the same, albeit with some quality-of-life changes; the ability to swap equipped items with one button is a huge upgrade to pausing and going into the menu every three seconds. I'm not saying that the remake is now the best way to play Ocarina of Time —there's something to be said for the friction that came with the original's technical limitations—but I am saying that the remake justifies its own existence with an attention to detail and a commitment to thrilling gameplay that shines through in every second of playtime.
In my time with the remake, I have learned to love the quirks and anxieties of a game that is rightfully considered among the very best to ever exist. I have also remembered that when Ocarina of Time gets something right, there's nothing like it. The puzzles are never too confusing, but they have a tactile pacing that makes every step towards the solution feel like a victory. The way the game teaches you to play it is unrivaled. It all fits like a perfect jigsaw, never throwing too much at the player while still challenging them to think creatively. I'm not one for adventure games in this vein anymore, which is probably why I have only played a few Zelda games since Ocarina and its sequel, but every time I opened a previously locked door, I had the forbidden thought of, "Should I play the whole Zelda series now?" There's no higher praise from me than saying Ocarina has me wondering if I should play Skyward Sword .
Ocarina of Time isn't the only blast from the past I've played recently. I have played World of Warcraft off and mostly on since early 2005, and I have tried every variation that the game has had to offer over that time. There is what people call "retail," which is the default game that has progressed from its messy origins to now, 11 expansions later. Retail these days feels like a completely different game than what I started playing, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. In 2019, Blizzard, the game's developers, caved to massive player pressure and released World of Warcraft Classic , essentially launching the game again from scratch, but with some changes to make it a bit more modern.
Classic was a big success, and has continued on since then. As the years of Classic went on, however, players wanted more. They wanted what was deemed " Classic Plus ," essentially the old game but with more twists and turns and new gameplay additions. Blizzard listened with Season of Discovery in 2023. This mode added a lot of abilities from later WoW as well as some new roles for long-time classes. For example, mages could now be healers and shamans could be grossly overpowered tanks. SoD was an even bigger success than Classic , all things considered, because it showed that the skeleton of WoW could support a new evolution.
That brings us to World of Warcraft: Forever , the new game mode that launched on Nov. 4 to record-breaking numbers. It seems that anyone and everyone who had ever played some form of WoW dipped into Forever to check it out. What is it, though? Forever is what Blizzard intends to be a different evolution of Classic . Classes got new tools and toys to play with, but they are not as wild as in SoD . Instead, Blizzard made everyone a bit stronger, a bit more fun to play, but still very much in the realm of old-school gameplay. The innovations instead seem to be coming from the new things players can do. Forever has added new zones in the open world, new dungeons to explore, and starting next month, new raids for groups of 10, 20, or 40 people.
In other words, Forever is an alternate timeline in which Blizzard decided to never release expansion packs, and instead keep everyone's max level at 60 and progress them horizontally. This allows the developers the ability to explore parts of the original world that were under-served, and turn them into new adventures with that Classic vibe. Forever is a much cozier game than what Retail WoW has become, much slower in its gameplay and progression. As the name implies, there is no rush here; this is meant to last as long as players keep logging in, and that makes everything feel more meaningful. The new weapon you got, or the new piece of armor, or a fancy trinket that gives you special powers ... all of those things are meant to, in some way or another, last for the duration of your character's lifespan, rather than getting replaced every four months with a new season.
I have not quit Retail WoW , but I fully took a break to dive into Forever when it released. In the two weeks since, I have played an obscene amount— Forever added viable controller support, so I've been playing on my laptop on the couch while watching TV—and have gotten my first character, a shaman, to level 60. It took me four days, 20 hours, and 29 minutes played to do so. Forever has taken over. Add in the roughly 12 hours of Ocarina of Time that have gotten me to the precipice of the Water Temple, and I've been living in video game past almost exclusively this month.
Though I've enjoyed wrapping myself in the warmth of nostalgia, what I've found most satisfying about this extended foray into the past is the usefulness of my familiarity. I'd consider myself an expert on leveling up characters in every version of WoW Classic at this point, so I was able to lock in and move my way from level 1 to 60 faster than anyone else I know. In Ocarina , my memories from two decades ago, as well as years of watching "BEST ZELDA DUNGEONS RANKED" YouTube videos, have come back to me and I am breezing through the game at a speed that would have befuddled my younger self. The Forest Temple is clearly the best dungeon in the game, and maybe in all of Zelda , but I steamrolled through all of the twisty hallways, tricky Poe mini-bosses, and the Phantom Ganon boss fight. As a child, that fight took me ages.
The ease with which these games have come back to me could have been a letdown, but I'm having a blast. My instincts are better, my stick skills have improved, and my reflexes, though worse than they were say in my early 20s, are more honed from so many hours of games. What these two excursions into my own gaming past have taught me is that I have really been on a journey of self-improvement—I see know lame that sounds—and the sense of accomplishment I get now is not from finishing something, but from finishing it in style.
It's interesting to me that I pregamed Grand Theft Auto VI , perhaps the most technologically advanced game of all time, with two dips into a simpler past. I don't know if I did i

articles.title_orig: China gives Japan PM frosty welcome at Apec amid fanfare for other leaders
articles.title_zh: China gives Japan PM frosty welcome at Apec amid fanfare for other leaders
articles.content_orig:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

articles.title_orig: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard disclose cyberattack on third-party vendors
articles.title_zh: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard disclose cyberattack on third-party vendors
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ), Visa ( V ), and Mastercard ( MA ) said on Thursday that some select customer data, including names and emails, was accessed by attackers after a cyberattack on a vendor.
Spokespeople for the companies said no payments or card data was leaked and that their own systems were not affected by the incident.
JPMorgan said it believes hackers who attacked a third-party vendor accessed marketing data, including customer names and email addresses. The bank also said the incident isn't related to outages many of its customers reported earlier this week, which it blamed on a software bug .
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," a JPMorgan spokesperson said.
"We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," a Mastercard spokesperson said. "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," the person added.
A Visa spokesperson added claims of the incident are associated to a third-party service provider in the Asia Pacific region.
"This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week," the Visa spokesperson added.
A ransomware group known as n0n has claimed responsibility for the attacks on the dark web and shared sample data as proof, according to cybersecurity firm SOCRadar.
The cybersecurity firm told Yahoo Finance that it hasn't independently verified whether the ransomware group carried out the intrusion. It also supported JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard's statements that the breaches most likely originated at a third-party vendor and involved marketing and benefit-program data such as names and email addresses.
"The most immediate risk for consumers is targeted phishing that impersonates their bank or card provider," SOCRadar chief information security officer Ensar Seker said in an emailed statement.
The latest incident comes as consumers are on high alert after a string of major technology outages this November . The Wall Street Journal earlier reported the connection between the breaches and the ransomware group.

articles.title_orig: AMD shares slide as report says China links could invite US scrutiny
articles.title_zh: AMD shares slide as report says China links could invite US scrutiny
articles.content_orig:
Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."
Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."
The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."
Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.
AMD continued to slide after-hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.content_orig:
It was the first-ever meeting of the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers—one that host Xi Jinping opened by hailing its “pioneering significance.”
Exactly what was achieved when Xi met with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump at Kylin Villa in northwestern Shenzhen on Thursday, however, has onlookers scratching their heads. Xi started by invoking the responsibility of Great Powers toward world peace; Putin delved into historic “shared interests;” while Trump immediately lashed out at “rogue globalist organisations,” such as the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The ICC “has gotten out of control,” Trump told his companions seated around a round wooden table, and has “really strayed far beyond its jurisdiction.”
It was almost as if this historic trilateral , held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, didn’t have any fixed agenda. It hadn’t. When the confab was first proposed, Putin wanted to talk about Ukraine, though U.S. officials pushed back. Trump instead suggested nuclear arms and Iran, but Beijing wasn’t keen. Finally, China’s Foreign Ministry settled on “safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations.”
It was therefore an occasion rich with platitudes but not a lot else. “In this global village, major countries shoulder special responsibilities,” said Xi, who also called for the destruction of all nuclear weapons. “Positive interaction among major powers is not an optional question, but a compulsory one.”
Still, the meeting served its purpose. Trump gained a chance to project influence after chastening midterms and the unfolding Nvidia saga that forced the resignation of his close friend Jensen Huang as CEO. Xi got to flaunt himself as the consummate statesman, while Putin took a baby step out from the diplomatic cold. But it was also a distinctly unsettling sight for the U.S. President to be sitting beside two of America’s most consequential adversaries, whose governments declared in 2022 that their friendship with each other had “no limits.”
Before the three-way meeting, Trump met separately with Putin and then Xi. His roughly 40 minutes with the Russian President began on a hopeful note: “Wonderful things can come out of this—or at least start,” Trump said. During an hour of talks with Xi, Trump returned to a more familiar concern. “I’ll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” he said. He also suggested that Washington and Beijing could work together to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
That prospect mattered to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said Wednesday that the war could end in a single meeting if the U.S. and China used their economic leverage against Moscow. Instead, Trump launched a broadside against the ICC, which has issued an arrest warrant against Putin for war crimes, urging his autocratic counterparts to cooperate on “ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty.”
Trump also said it was “vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world,” before segueing into a justification of his war in Iran : “That’s what we’re doing in Iran. We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Of course, this was always going to be an occasion that would put style over substance. On Wednesday, Xi surprised onlookers by greeting a clearly delighted Trump on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan Airport. Their handshake turned into a brief hug, before five People’s Liberation Army J-10C fighter jets flew overhead, billowing red, yellow, and blue smoke.
In personally meeting Trump as he deplaned Air Force One, Xi reciprocated the welcome he received from the U.S. President at Joint Base Andrews in September. The gesture was a first by a top Chinese leader since Mao Zedong met Nikita Khrushchev at Beijing’s airport in 1959.
Putin had to suffice with being greeted by Xi’s chief of staff, Cai Qi, upon his earlier arrival in the wee hours of Wednesday morning. But Xi spent much of that afternoon in talks with his embattled Russian counterpart, who used his speech to assembled CEOs to lambast Western sanctions, crowing that the U.S. and Europe had “punished themselves” with punitive measures, which Russia had successfully sidestepped anyway.
Upon emerging from his two-hour bilateral with Putin, Xi called on both countries to “lead and advance … the democratization of international relations.” Putin, in turn, boasted that economic coercion was “a thing of the past.” Later in the evening, Putin and Trump shook hands before the gala dinner as Xi looked on smiling.
“Beijing’s top priority would be to create a more stable external environment for China’s development, particularly by making relations with Washington more predictable while maintaining steady cooperation with Moscow,” says Sun Chenghao, a fellow with Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy.
Still, the summit threatened to be overshadowed by the Nvidia scandal, with company founder Huang admitting an affair with a woman accused of illicitly funneling chips to China and whom U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly suspect may be a Chinese spy. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued an interim rule aimed at stopping Chinese firms from accessing advanced U.S. chips through data centers abroad.
Trump told Fox News that he and Xi “spoke the whole evening” during Wednesday’s gala dinner but only “briefly” discussed Nvidia. Trump also claimed he was unaware of the espionage allegations, which China vehemently denies. “I haven’t heard that she was a spy,” Trump said. “She was a businesswoman who bought chips, and who knows if they were bought right or wrong.”
Trump also appeared to shoot down any hopes of regulation governing AI: “We oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control or stifle [AI], and we won’t allow that to happen,” he said.
Still, the historic trilateral did succeed in visibly placing China at the center of Great Power diplomacy. Hosting the leaders alongside APEC supports Beijing’s claim that global influence is shifting eastward, with China as a stabilizing power, particularly amid unpredictable U.S. policy.
“The optics might actually play well for China,” says Chong Ja Ian, a professor of international relations at the National University of Singapore. “It certainly would fit the sort of image that Beijing and Xi would like to create for themselves.”
But while APEC was created in 1989 to ease trade and investment across the region, today’s world has been gripped by rising protectionism. The Trump Administration has levied tariffs on 60 trading partners that together account for 99.4% of U.S. imports, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. Moreover, Europe is increasingly chary about cheap Chinese exports that Brussels says are fueled by subsidies and industrial overcapacity.
Xi used his Wednesday address to business leaders to promise a more open Chinese market and present the world’s second-largest economy as a source of opportunity. “History tells us that opening doors brings progress while closing doors leaves one behind,” he said.
Yet the image of three elderly leaders debating global problems behind closed doors sits uneasily beside Xi’s call for a more multipolar world. Pro-Kremlin media was especially keen to frame the meeting as Yalta 2.0 after the historic powwow between Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill toward the end of World War II.
But it is Ukraine’s plucky defiance of that invasion that underscores how today’s Middle Powers have more agency. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged third countries to work together on trade, security and technology in order to shape the rules and resist economic coercion. “Middle powers must act together because if you are not at the table, you are on the menu,” Carney said.

articles.title_orig: Europe rejects 'Yalta 2.0' for Ukraine after Trump meets Putin and Xi
articles.title_zh: Europe rejects 'Yalta 2.0' for Ukraine after Trump meets Putin and Xi
articles.content_orig:
European leaders have forcefully rejected any attempts to re-enact the 1945 Yalta Conference to end Russia's war on Ukraine and split the continent into spheres of influence.
The pushback went public on Thursday at a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, comprising Kyiv's allies, hosted by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The gathering in Berlin took place just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping held a historic trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, dubbed "Yalta 2.0" by media commentators.
Trump, Putin and Xi discussed Ukraine, but their joint statement, titled "Declaration Toward Peace", did not mention the country.
"A Yalta format will not bring peace," Merz said, flanked by other leaders.
"At Yalta, Europe was divided up. It was parcelled up. And we won't allow anything like that to happen again."
Merz gifted the over 40 delegations that took part in the talks a piece of the Berlin Wall, which, he said, is "what Yalta represented".
By his side, French President Emmanuel Macron said the four-point statement issued by Trump, Putin and Xi in Shenzhen did not replicate the outcome of the 1945 conference, which set the stage for the four-decade-long Cold War.
"I don't think that it amounts to a reorganisation of the world," he said.
"If there is one critical element for the reorganisation of Europe and its security, it is the meeting that took place (today) in Berlin."
Macron stressed that negotiations to end the war would need to involve Ukraine, Europe, the US and Russia seated at the same table.
"Europeans have taken decisions. They have decided to determine their own fate," the French president said. "Europe is not a subject on a menu of discussions, but a series of powers who want to build their own future".
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham echoed Macron's message, saying "there is no decision about Ukraine without Ukraine in the room (and) there's no decision about European security without Europe represented in the room".
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the meeting in Berlin bore "testament" to Russia's failure to sow division among European allies.
The four leaders agreed that the time has come for Europe to engage in face-to-face negotiations with Russia, marking a step that has yet to take place in the negotiation process.
Europe has appointed a joint team of seven representatives from France, the UK, Germany, Poland, Italy, the EU institutions and NATO for the next round of talks.
US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who flew to Berlin to attend the meeting, also called on Russia to allow European participation.
"We do believe that having Europe at the table will be essential to ending this war in a just and long-term, durable way," Kushner said at the closing press conference.
"And the Russians are willing to trust that instinct on our behalf."
Moscow, though, has not committed to a multilateral format.
Speaking in Shenzhen, Putin said he had suggested "via diplomatic channels that the Europeans come to Moscow to define their positions," and, after that, the Kremlin would "decide on continuing the dialogue with Ukraine".
Putin also said that it "would be strange to discuss Europe's security without Europe itself", referring to the demands that Moscow has tabled to restructure the continent's security architecture, which Macron slammed as "maximalist".
Merz said the debate on European security would happen only after peace has been established in Ukraine. The future security guarantees to the war-weary country will inherently have "repercussions" for the transatlantic alliance, he said.
Among the guarantees in the works is a clause emulating NATO's Article 5 of collective defence should Russia attack Ukraine again. Another guarantee would be a Europe-led peacekeeping force, which Putin says he would not allow in any scenario.
"From America's perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal," Kushner said. "And I think that that's something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America's interest to do that."
During the closed-door discussions in Berlin, Trump phoned in from his plane and addressed the room, Kushner confirmed. Media reports suggest that Trump expressed scepticism about Europe's military support for Ukraine.
Leaders seemed unmoved and agreed that assistance will continue unabated to put Ukraine in a strong position at the negotiating table.
"I hope that message is heard very clearly in Moscow," Burnham said.
"For as long as it takes, we will be there at the side of Ukraine, and we will not falter. Our support will be unwavering. And that's the biggest weapon we have together."

articles.title_orig: TSMC tightens China AI chip curbs as new US rules close manufacturing loophole, sources say
articles.title_zh: TSMC tightens China AI chip curbs as new US rules close manufacturing loophole, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. As of May, there had been 3.4 million requested sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices .
"Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents.
The Commerce Department, AMD and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
"The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks continued.
The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China.
In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.
Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS —  Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions.
"Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting.
Maginfra and New Matrix did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2.
Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify.
Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third controls.
The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.

articles.title_orig: US mortgage rates rise for the first time in five weeks
articles.title_zh: US mortgage rates rise for the first time in five weeks
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates are climbing again after a few weeks of easing following a three-year high.
The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 7.28% this week, up from 7.11% last week, according to Freddie Mac. It’s the largest one-week jump since the week of October 1.
That’s also more than a full percentage point jump compared to this time last year, when the average was 6.26%.
Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield, which moved higher recently after a hotter-than-expected inflation report increased the odds that the Federal Reserve could hike its benchmark interest rate at its December policy meeting.
Mortgage rates have now stayed stubbornly over 7% since late September – the highest they’ve been at any time since 2000 – aside from a single month in 2023.
That has further pumped the brakes on an already stalled housing market. Pending home sales, which measures home transactions that haven’t officially closed yet, collapsed in October to a record low, according to a report released by the National Association of Realtors on Wednesday. Pending deals fell 4.7% between September and October, and nearly 17% year-over-year.
“It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million,” said Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist, in a statement. “Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.”

articles.title_orig: Trump says no rush on Iran decision, looks to next year
articles.title_zh: Trump says no rush on Iran decision, looks to next year
articles.content_orig:
Iran's foreign ministry rejected President Trump's accusations the country is developing chemical or biological weapons and compared the situation to then-Secretary of State Colin Powell asserting Iraq had weapons of mass destruction.
"After the grand narrative of the 'Iranian nuclear threat,' U.S. officials are now claiming that there are indications Iran is developing biological or chemical weapons!" Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X . "The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar. Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia."
Baqaei raised the specter of the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003 over alleged development of weapons of mass destruction by Saddam Hussein's government and asked why Americans would fall for it again.
"Do American officials really expect the world to forget Colin Powell's infamous appearance before the U.N. Security Council in 2003, when he held up a small vial as a visual representation of the alleged threat posed by Iraq's weapons of mass destruction?" the spokesperson said. "That moment has since become an enduring symbol of one of the most consequential intelligence failures and political deceptions in modern history."
He added, "And now we find ourselves facing ominous new allegations and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script."
Mr. Trump on Wednesday had claimed there was an "indication" Iran was looking to develop chemical or biological weapons because the U.S. had "shut them out" of obtaining nuclear weapons.
"They're looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear," Mr. Trump told a Fox reporter in Shenzhen, China.
The Senate rejected a House-adopted resolution aimed at reining in President Trump's ability to strike Iran, losing Republican support despite frustration with the war following the party's losses in the midterm elections.
In a 48 to 51 vote, three Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky — joined all but one Senate Democrat — Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania — in support of the measure.
Thursday's vote marked the first time either chamber has weighed in on the war since the midterm elections, which dealt Republicans sweeping losses. Voters cited the war in Iran, and its toll on the economy, as among their top concerns.
The resolution would have directed the president "to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran," but its impact would have been largely symbolic.
Iraqi forces will begin deploying on Friday in the main stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group, state media reported, as Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi steps up efforts to rein in the faction.
Kataeb Hezbollah on Tuesday adopted a softer tone toward the U.S.-backed premier, with Iraqi sources saying a compromise was reached during a visit by Iranian commander Esmail Qaani.
Iraq has faced mounting U.S. pressure to curb Iran's influence and contain Tehran-backed armed groups — a difficult task in a country long caught between its two allies.
Tensions have grown between Zaidi and Kataeb Hezbollah since the U.S.-backed leader vowed to disarm Iran-backed groups that have long-targeted U.S. interests in the region — a longstanding American demand but a tall order for Baghdad.
This week, Zaidi gave Kataeb Hezbollah a deadline to withdraw from Jurf al-Sakher, also known as Jurf al-Nasr, which lies south of Baghdad, after the government said an investigative committee had confirmed oil smuggling in the area — a claim the armed group denied.
President Trump told Channel 12 News in Israel that he is in no hurry to make any decisions on the war with Iran, and could in fact wait until next year.
"I'm not rushing to make any decisions on Iran," Mr. Trump told Keshet 12's Barak Ravid, who spoke to the president as he returned from China. "We'll see what happens after the new year starts."
The story noted Mr. Trump could also change his mind, though.
The tone seems in line with his and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's comments from last week. Mr. Trump called new strikes "quite unlikely," while Rubio said new strikes weren't needed since the economic sanctions campaign was working so well.
In an interview with Fox News on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said he had no need to ask China or Russia for help with an Iran deal.
"They want to make a deal, so I don't need help," Mr. Trump told the network. "I mean, I'm not going to go in asking for help. And frankly, they've treated us very well. They haven't fired. They haven't put ships in the water."
The war against Iran has cost the U.S. military more than $48 billion since the conflict began in late February, a Pentagon official said Thursday.
"That number includes munitions, equipment replacement costs, and operational cost," Arthur Miller, the Pentagon's deputy comptroller, told lawmakers during a hearing on his nomination as assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management.
The figure does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, some of which have been hit hard by Iranian drone and missile attacks, nor does it take into account the harm to the global economy.
The update was the first since mid-October, when the war's cost was pegged at $47.1 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News. The bulk of that price tag at the time was replacing used munitions at about $29 billion. Lost equipment, including planes and unmanned aircraft, accounted for about $6 billion.
Iran said Thursday that it will not accept "unconditional and unlimited cooperation" with inspectors from the United Nations' International Atomic Energy Agency while it is being bombed.
"We do not accept being targeted on the one hand and being asked in a demanding tone on the other to provide accurate information about our materials and facilities and to provide unlimited access to them," Reza Najafi, Iran's ambassador and permanent representative to the United Nations and international organizations in Vienna, said Thursday, according to Iran's semi-official ISNA news agency.
"While adhering to its obligations, Iran will not accept unconditional and unlimited cooperation with the Agency [IAEA] and will review each inspection request on a case-by-case basis, taking into account security conditions," he added.
The nuclear issue, including IAEA access to Iran's nuclear sites, has been a key sticking point in negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
President Trump has justified the war as a necessary action to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Iran has always denied any nuclear weapons aspirations, but it has enriched uranium to near-weapons grade. The exact whereabouts and condition of that material, and the circumstances of many facilities themselves, have remained unclear since the U.S. and Israel launched a major attack on the sites in June 2025. Iran has refused IAEA access to its nuclear facilities since then.
Saudi Arabia has condemned Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen for targeting a skyscraper in the financial district of Riyadh, the kingdom's capital.
"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs expresses the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's strong condemnation and denunciation of the continued terrorist attacks by the Houthi terrorist militia targeting civilian and economic facilities and civilian objects in the capital, Riyadh, and the resulting material damage to the King Abdullah Financial District," the ministry wrote in a post on X .
Earlier, Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency said the building was damaged in a Houthi strike but that there were no injuries.
The Iran-backed Houthis struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district on Thursday, causing damage but no injuries, Saudi authorities said.

articles.title_orig: Trump calls Putin and Xi friends. They have other plans.
articles.title_zh: Trump calls Putin and Xi friends. They have other plans.
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries, but there appeared to be little concrete to show for the meeting in terms of resolving any of the crises facing the world.
The leaders offered a joint statement after their roughly hour-and-a-half-long meeting. Mr. Trump immediately left for his return flight to the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. On the flight home, the president said on social media he will hold a press conference at noon on Friday to discuss the trip.
The presidents discussed Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine , which Mr. Trump has wanted to bring to a negotiated end. But the only significant statement on the conflict came after the meeting from Putin, who ruled out any direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing a major strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces on a key bridge in Russian-held Crimea.
Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it called a joint statement from all three leaders characterizing the talks. The White House later provided the same statement.
The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."
They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the " International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."
Finally, the leaders "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."
The White House indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.
The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.
Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine, who sits on the Committee on Foreign Relations, said the image of Mr. Trump standing with Xi and Putin was concerning.
"Some of the pictures troubled me, seeing the president stand with Putin and Xi, rather than seeing the president stand with the leaders of the global democracies," Kaine said. "When I saw them, it turned my stomach a bit, and particularly President Trump's declaration that Vladimir Putin was a friend. Vladimir Putin is not a friend, and so you know he was either being insincere or he is deeply deluded if he thinks Vladimir Putin is a friend."
In a phone call with NBC reporter Gabe Gutierrez, Mr. Trump called the meeting a 12 on a scale of zero to 10.
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
After the trilateral talks Thursday, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.
"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."
Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia  in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."
Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."
Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons , with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.
Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program , ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year .
China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi , however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."
The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.
A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence .
The summit took place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang , whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed , is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.
Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.

☀️ Good morning from The Legal File! Here is the rundown of today's top legal news:
The Big Law salary war is heating up once again. Associates at more major US law firms are getting raises, cementing a new market rate at top firms that ranges from $235,000 for first-year lawyers to $455,000 for senior associates, with additional bonus pay.
Cravath, Swaine & Moore on November 17 matched rival Milbank's new associate salary scale while also handing out higher bonuses, according to an internal Cravath memo published by the website Above the Law. The move spurred Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson and Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton to follow suit on November 18, according to internal memos viewed by Reuters.
Milbank in June raised associate salaries to a new range starting at $235,000 up to $455,000 based on seniority. The New York firm, which has been a first mover among large law firms on associate compensation, in July rolled out so-called special bonuses for associates between $6,000 and $25,000.
Top law firms typically move quickly to match salaries and bonuses to stay competitive. A handful of law firms matched Milbank's salaries over the summer and in recent weeks , but other major firms, including key ones in New York whose compensation scales are closely followed by the industry, had not yet announced any changes before this week.
President Trump's nominees to fill two vacancies at the US Securities and Exchange Commission are scheduled for confirmation hearings before a US Senate panel, in what would end a longstanding leadership vacuum at Wall Street's top regulator, should they be confirmed.
Republican Steven Levine, a former aide to current Republican Commissioner Mark Uyeda at the SEC, and Democrat Kristin Johnson, a former member of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, are slated to appear before the Senate Banking Committee.
The Trump administration has since shrunk the SEC's workforce and sharply scaled back enforcement while ushering in new financial products based on digital assets that Democrats say are risky. Paul Atkins, the current chair, has also pursued a deregulatory agenda that enhances corporations' power and limits traditional avenues for shareholder activism.
Trump nominated Levine and Johnson on November 12 after previously resisting Senate Democrats' calls to fill bipartisan vacancies at the SEC and CFTC. The five-seat SEC currently has only two members, both Republicans.
Two US government lawyers violated professional conduct rules in their use of artificial intelligence, including the disclosure of confidential documents to a public AI platform and misleading statements made to a judge about how AI-generated errors appeared in a court filing, according to a Justice Department ethics office.
The DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility on November 17 issued summaries describing the incidents while leaving out details including the names of the lawyers, where they worked and whether they are still employed by the department.
The cases offer a rare window into how the DOJ is policing its lawyers' use of generative AI as the technology rapidly spreads through the legal profession, creating confidentiality, accuracy and compliance challenges for courts, law firms and government agencies.
In both cases, the office’s findings were referred to the department’s Professional Misconduct Review Unit, which has the power to discipline misconduct.
Major US law firms are continuing to scoop up lawyers from Weil, Gotshal & Manges, including more than two dozen new partner hires by Sidley Austin, Skadden, Simpson Thacher, Dechert and Kirkland & Ellis.
Weil lawyers are scattering following the firm's decision this month to wind down operations, boosting partnerships at its onetime competitors. Partners at Weil voted on November 10 to dissolve the firm after mounting departures, cementing the fall of a 95-year-old law firm that helped steer high-profile bankruptcies, corporate takeovers and litigation for decades.
The moves add to an already busy hiring market for law firms that's been supercharged by Weil's collapse. Earlier this week Cleary Gottlieb , Paul Hastings and Skadden said they were bringing on other lawyers from Weil.
Skadden said November 18 that it was adding a team of 11 restructuring partners as well as seven intellectual property partners from Weil. Matt Barr, who led Weil's vaunted restructuring practice, will become the head of Skadden's global restructuring group, with about 40 Weil restructuring and corporate attorneys joining in all.
Sidley said it hired 14 partners from Weil, including its M&A head and corporate department co-chair Michael Lubowitz, US private equity practice co-head Peter Feist, corporate co-managing partner Lyuba Goltser, banking and finance co-head Andrew Colao, tech and IP transactions head Charan Sandhu, and US privacy and cybersecurity head Olivia Greer.
👋 That's all for today, thank you for reading The Legal File , and have a great day!

The Razr Flex will compete with the iPhone Duo, Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, and other widescreen folding devices.﻿
New leaked images of Motorola’s next folding smartphone shared by SammyGuru add more credence to the theory that widescreen could be the default design for foldables moving forward. Following a single leaked shot shared to Reddit yesterday , this new crop of images reveal the Motorola Razr Flex from several angles in two finishes with its inner screen completely open and partially folded.
The photos show the Razr Flex in two finishes: coriander brown and dark botanical garden, according to SammyGuru . The brown option features a back panel with a bumpy leather-like finish, while the green has a fabric-like woven finish. The cover screen has a hole-punch selfie camera centered at the top, while the Razr Flex’s inner screen pushes the camera to the upper right corner. On the back is a pill-shaped bar with two cameras and a flash.
The Flex is expected to be a smaller and more affordable alternative to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 , which has a 5.5-inch cover screen and a 7.6-inch main display when unfolded. But more specific details — including the size of the Razr Flex, its pricing, and when it’s expected to be debut — are still unknown.

articles.title_orig: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
articles.title_zh: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you
articles.content_orig:
Google on Thursday announced that it is bringing computer use to its Gemini desktop application on macOS, allowing its AI to complete tasks on users’ behalf, navigating native Mac apps, and browsing websites in the background.
The tech giant is a little late to the game with this launch, as other leading AI model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta have already been offering agentic features in their desktop applications for some time. Meanwhile, Google only this week announced the broader rollout of Gemini’s “Tasks,” the in-app feature that allows the AI to work more as an agent, helping users sign into websites, make online purchases, or book appointments.
Google also only recently began admitting early testers to try its revamped “CC” AI agent, announced in September , which is designed to help families stay organized across email, calendars, chats, and tasks.
Computer use is another type of agentic offering that allows an AI agent to take actions directly on the user’s computer — in Gemini’s case, a Mac. This allows the AI to complete multistep tasks that involve getting things done across local files, apps, and the web. After the user instructs the AI what they want to do, they’ll see the agent working in a live preview in their chat, while still keeping their screen and cursor free to continue working on other things.
As with other AI agents offering computer use, users can pause, stop, and approve Gemini’s actions before they happen.
Google suggests the feature could be useful for tedious tasks and other workflows, like filling out forms, repeating the same task over and over across a batch of files, organizing files into folders based on specific criteria, creating slideshows from files or information in online dashboards, and more.
The feature is initially available in English in the U.S. and requires the Gemini app for Mac and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription. The company didn’t say when it would expand to other markets or platforms.

articles.title_orig: How To Game Share GTA 6 And Split The Cost With A Friend
articles.title_zh: How To Game Share GTA 6 And Split The Cost With A Friend
articles.content_orig:
You can do this on Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5.
Even if you've been eagerly awaiting the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 , shelling out $80 for the standard edition or $100 for the ultimate edition isn't easy for everyone. You shouldn't expect the biggest game of the year to go on sale any time soon, but the good news is there's another way to save some money on it. The only catch is that you need a friend who wants to play the game on the same kind of console and is willing to split the cost with you.
Both Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5 have a game sharing feature that lets you play one copy of a game on two different consoles. While there are some restrictions on sharing DLC and other in-game items, most full games can be shared, and GTA 6 is no exception.
On PlayStation 5, sharing works by signing into your account on two different consoles and enabling the console sharing feature. After buying GTA 6 , sign into your PlayStation account on the console you want to share the game with. Open Settings on the console's main screen, then go to Users and Accounts and select Other . Open Console Sharing and Offline Play and toggle the feature on.
While logged into your account, your friend can now download any of your games to their own console, then switch back to their own account to play the game. Keep in mind that your account can only share games with one other console at a time. Your friend will also need to remember to switch back to their own account after starting to download one of your games, since you can't use the same account on two consoles simultaneously. Once you've set up console sharing, your friend will maintain access to your library permanently unless you change your password.
The process for sharing GTA 6 on Xbox Series X is similar, but works by designating one console as your home Xbox. As with the PS5, you should first buy the game, then log into your account on your friend's Xbox. From the main screen, open Settings from the top menu, then select General > Personalization > My home Xbox and select the box marked Make this my home Xbox . Now you can download GTA 6 to the console, and your friend can switch back to their account to play it there.
This will allow anyone using this Xbox to download games on your account without you signing in. In the menu itself, a note recommends making your own console your home Xbox, but that would only allow another user to play GTA 6 on your own console . Also note that you can only switch your home Xbox five times per year, so be mindful of that limit if you want to change who you're sharing games with.

articles.title_orig: White House pool have phones taken away on return from China as speculation mounts over unscheduled stop
articles.title_zh: White House pool have phones taken away on return from China as speculation mounts over unscheduled stop
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
White House reporters traveling aboard Air Force One had their phones temporarily confiscated before President Donald Trump’s plane took off after his trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, raising the specter of an unscheduled detour on his way back to Washington D.C.
U.S. officials collected reporters’ devices as the president’s plane prepared to leave Shenzhen, China, Thursday evening.
“At 6:45 pm consider this your wheels up,” the White House pool report read. “Our phones are being taken away for now for security reasons.”
No one on the trip has provided more information. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for more information.
It is highly unusual for reporters’ phones to be sequestered outside of situations when the president is traveling to a war zone, such as when Trump flew to Al Asad Air Base in Iraq at Christmas in 2018, and to Bagram Air Field in Afghanistan for Thanksgiving in 2019.
Fox News correspondent Jacqui Heinrich, the current president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, pointed out on X that the pool’s phones were not taken when Trump left Beijing after his state visit in May.
The move was later explained as a cybersecurity measure, as the phones used by journalists in China were placed in a metal-lined Faraday bag to prevent them from emitting any signals while the aircraft was aloft.
Most of the devices that were collected were so-called burner phones used only for the travel to China, as journalists had previously stored their regular devices in similar bags aboard Air Force One for use during the Philippines leg of the trip and while en route to Washington.
Separately, a flight restriction that had been imposed over Alaska around the time Air Force One had been scheduled to refuel there was lifted Thursday, raising questions as to the plane’s destination.
The most obvious candidate for a detour was North Korea. Trump spent the days before the summit musing that Kim Jong Un might join him when he met with China ’s Xi and Russia ’s Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in Manila that the president was “prepared” to meet the North Korean leader.
“It may not happen, but he’s prepared to do it,” Rubio said.
However on a call with reporters before the trip, senior U.S. officials said there were “no plans at all for engagement with North Korea.”
Trump relished the pageantry and attention that were lavished on his first two meetings with Kim, though neither sit-down resulted in the denuclearization deals he had promised to reach with the brutal autocrat.
He also met Kim for a third time during a visit to the Korean Demilitarized Zone and briefly became the first American president to set foot in North Korea.
The intrigue surrounding the president’s departure from China followed Trump’s participation in the first-ever meeting between an American president and the autocrats who have led the other two major nuclear powers for a combined 41 years.
Trump gave Putin a warm reception when he met with him for a bilateral meeting immediately preceding the three-way sit-down.
The U.S. president pointed, smiled and called out “Who is that? He’s my friend!” as he walked into a room with his Russian counterpart. The scene was captured by TV cameras that had been permitted in, even as journalists were barred from attending to prevent the leaders from being asked any uncomfortable questions, though a Russian official attributed the move to space constraints.
Trump said of Putin: “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they’ll come out of this.”
The Kremlin said after the meeting that the pair had discussed the ongoing war in Ukraine , and that Putin left in an “excellent” mood.
The White House offered no official readout of the sit-down, which lasted approximately 40 minutes.
Following the trilateral meeting, the Russian, Chinese and American governments released a four-point “peace declaration” reaffirming that a nuclear war should never be fought and vowing to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks.
The three leaders also pledged to advance reforms of the United Nations, to increase supplies of refined petroleum products for all countries and to uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.
The International Criminal Court in The Hague has issued arrest warrants for Putin and five other Russian officials. The Trump administration has been working to delegitimize and defund the ICC out of fear that Trump and his associates could be subject to war crimes charges over America’s campaign of airstrikes against alleged drug smugglers or an airstrike against an Iranian school that left over 100 children dead.

articles.title_zh: Trump questions Europe's billions in Ukraine aid during surprise call
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump has “sharply questioned” European countries over their continued financial support for Ukraine during the country’s conflict with Russia.
The president unexpectedly phoned into a meeting of Ukraine’s European allies on Thursday, according to the Politico publication, which heard from four European officials who were briefed on the discussion.
He asked the allies why they were continuing to spend billions on military support for Kyiv.
The call came mere hours after Trump wrapped up a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Chinese counterpart, President Xi Jinping, in Shenzhen, China.
The US president is said to have called Berlin from his private aircraft, Air Force One, and insisted that Putin was serious about future peace negotiations about Ukraine.
Three of the European officials, who have been granted anonymity, said that Trump was strongly sceptical about the possibility of further aid being provided to Ukraine by the Coalition of the Willing, an alliance of 34 countries – plus Ukraine – who have pledged strengthened support for Ukraine against Russian aggression.
One of the officials said Trump bemoaned the fact that a lot of people are dying in the conflict, and a lot of money is being “wasted” on the nearly five-year-long war. That official also confirmed that the US leader believes Putin will cooperate with peace negotiations with Ukraine.
This is a developing story.
